q: A client runs BEGIN and UPDATE, then disconnects without COMMIT. A new connection finds the old value. What does that show?
options: Atomicity working: the unfinished transaction counts for nothing
A failure of atomicity: the update was lost
A failure of durability: the write wasn't flushed in time
An isolation anomaly: the new connection read a stale snapshot
why: A lost connection is treated as a rollback. My notes called this a failure of atomicity, which is backwards.

q: One statement in a Postgres transaction fails a CHECK constraint. What happens to the next SELECT in that transaction?
options: It fails with 'current transaction is aborted', until ROLLBACK
It runs normally, and only the failed statement is undone
It runs, and returns the values from before the transaction
It waits until the application decides whether to commit
why: After an error Postgres refuses further commands, and even COMMIT answers ROLLBACK. MySQL undoes only the failed statement, which is why engines need testing.

q: You set READ UNCOMMITTED on Postgres and watch for a dirty read. What do you see?
options: None: Postgres accepts the level and runs it as read committed
A dirty read, as the SQL standard requires at this level
An error, because Postgres doesn't accept that level
A dirty read only if the other transaction later commits
why: The docs call that the only sensible mapping onto MVCC. MySQL really implements the level: its total went from 330 to 630 and back.

q: What separates a phantom read from a non-repeatable read?
options: A row you read changes in one, and a new matching row appears in the other
One reads uncommitted data, and the other reads committed data
One needs SERIALIZABLE to occur, and the other needs READ COMMITTED
They're the same anomaly, under two names from different standards
why: That's why locking the rows you read can stop a non-repeatable read and not a phantom: the new row didn't exist to lock.

q: A report prints lines that add up to 330 and a footer that says 830, in one transaction at read committed. Why?
options: Each statement got its own snapshot, and a commit landed between them
The second statement read uncommitted data from the writer
The report's transaction was aborted and silently retried
The footer query used a stale index that hadn't been vacuumed
why: Nothing was dirty. The two statements just describe two moments. Repeatable read gives both one snapshot.

q: Why does Postgres's repeatable read show no phantoms, though the SQL standard allows them there?
options: It's implemented as snapshot isolation, so the whole transaction reads one snapshot
It locks the whole table for the length of the transaction
It runs repeatable read transactions one at a time
It checks for phantoms at commit and retries them silently
why: The standard sets a minimum. Snapshots give the stronger behaviour for free.

q: How does Postgres provide a snapshot without copying the table?
options: Row versions record the transactions that made and ended them, and a snapshot lists which count as finished
It keeps a hidden copy of each page that changed since the transaction began
It blocks writers until all the readers have finished
It stores old values in an undo log and rebuilds rows on read
why: Old versions stay in the table. That's MVCC, and it's why reading never blocks writing.

q: At repeatable read on MySQL, a plain count says 2, then SELECT ... FOR SHARE in the same transaction says 3. Why?
options: Locking reads see the latest committed rows, and only plain SELECTs use the snapshot
FOR SHARE starts a new transaction with a new snapshot
The first count missed a row because of a stale index
InnoDB's snapshot expires after a fixed number of statements
why: The docs say the snapshot applies to SELECT, not necessarily to DML. An UPDATE there works on the latest rows too.

q: Two sessions read 10 units and write back computed values, 7 and 8, at repeatable read. What happened on each engine?
options: Postgres failed the second write with a serialization error, and MySQL let it overwrite the first
Both failed the second write with a serialization error
Both let the second write overwrite the first
MySQL failed the second write, and Postgres let it overwrite the first
why: Same level name, same steps, different results. Test isolation behaviour on the engine you run.

q: Which change fixes the stock-count lost update even at read committed?
options: UPDATE stock SET units = units - 3, so the database does the arithmetic on the current row
Reading the value twice before writing it
Adding an index on the units column
Setting synchronous_commit to on
why: The waiting UPDATE recomputes from the row the first transaction committed, so 5 units remain. The read-then-write in the application is what lost the sale.

q: Two on-call doctors each see two on call and take themselves off. Why doesn't repeatable read stop this?
options: They wrote different rows, so no write conflict exists: the conflict is between a read and a write
Repeatable read only protects primary key columns
Their transactions were on separate connections, which aren't compared
Boolean columns aren't covered by snapshot isolation
why: That's write skew. Only SERIALIZABLE, or locking the rows you read, stops it.

q: How does Postgres's SERIALIZABLE stop write skew?
options: It tracks what each transaction read, with locks that don't block, and fails one at commit
It runs transactions strictly one after another
It takes shared locks on everything read, so writers wait
It locks the whole table for each transaction
why: Those locks show up as SIReadLock. The loser gets a serialization error and must retry.

q: The same doctors at SERIALIZABLE on MySQL ended with a deadlock error. Why?
options: InnoDB turns plain SELECTs into FOR SHARE, so each update waited on the other's shared lock
MySQL's SERIALIZABLE is implemented with a single global lock
The two transactions used different isolation levels by accident
InnoDB detected write skew and labelled it as a deadlock
why: That's lock-based serializable, which is what my notes described as if it were universal. The rule held by a different route.

q: Which is the fair trade between SERIALIZABLE and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE?
options: Serializable keeps concurrency and needs retry code, and FOR UPDATE queues work but rarely fails
Serializable is always slower, and FOR UPDATE is always safer
Serializable needs no application changes, and FOR UPDATE needs a retry loop
They're the same thing with different syntax
why: Optimistic against pessimistic. Which wins depends on how often conflicts really happen.

q: A pictures table says 5 likes, and picture_likes holds 2 rows. Which meaning of consistency is broken?
options: Consistency in data: the stored data breaks a rule, though nothing crashed
Consistency in reads: a replica hasn't caught up yet
Isolation: another transaction read uncommitted data
Durability: some rows weren't flushed to disk
why: The database can only enforce rules you declare. The second meaning, reads seeing the latest write, is about copies.

q: What has to reach disk before COMMIT returns in Postgres?
options: The WAL records for the transaction, forced there with fsync
Every data page the transaction changed
Both the WAL and the data pages, in one write
Nothing: the OS cache is treated as durable
why: Only the log needs to be safe. Data pages are written later, at a checkpoint, and the log can rebuild them.

q: Why isn't a successful write() call enough for durability?
options: The OS may hold the data in its cache, so power loss can lose it until fsync confirms
write() is asynchronous and can fail silently without any error
write() only updates file metadata, not contents
Disks can't accept writes smaller than one page
why: fsync forces the data onto the disk and waits. That wait is the real cost of a commit.

q: With synchronous_commit=off, a killed server lost 23, 24 and 161 acknowledged commits. What didn't happen?
options: No transaction was left half done: only the most recent commits went missing
Nothing was lost from before the server started that day
No commits were lost once the server was restarted cleanly
No client saw an error at all, either before or after the crash
why: The database stays consistent. You lose the last moments of data, bounded by three times wal_writer_delay.

q: In one run, 1,079 commits were acknowledged and 1,080 rows survived. What does the extra row mean?
options: That commit reached disk, and the server died before the reply got back
A row was duplicated during crash recovery
The client's counter was off by one because of a race
A background process inserted a row during restart
why: A client can't tell a lost reply from a lost write. That's why retries need idempotency.

q: Why can't a container kill test what a power cut does?
options: The OS survives a process kill, so its page cache isn't lost
Containers write directly to disk, with no cache at all
Docker takes a snapshot of memory before killing a process
SIGKILL gives the database time to flush its buffers
why: The losses there came from Postgres's own memory. Real power loss would need different hardware to test.

q: Which phenomenon isn't in the SQL standard's table, yet is perhaps the most dangerous?
options: Lost update
Dirty read
Non-repeatable read
Phantom read
why: It was formalised later, in A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels. It raises no error anywhere.

q: What does error code 40001 tell an application to do on Postgres?
options: Run the whole transaction again from a fresh read
Repeat only the statement that failed
Commit, because the error is only a warning
Raise the isolation level and carry on
why: It's a serialization failure. Retrying only the last statement would reuse a stale view.

q: A rolled-back INSERT used id 7, so the next row gets id 8. Why?
options: Sequence changes aren't rolled back, so gaps in ids are normal
Postgres reserves the rolled-back id for later reuse in that session
The row with id 7 is still in the table, marked as hidden
The sequence skips numbers to avoid conflicts with replicas
why: The docs note this. Making sequences transactional would serialise every insert.

q: Why does a long read-only transaction cost something, even though it writes nothing?
options: Its snapshot keeps old row versions alive, so they can't be cleaned up
It holds an exclusive lock on every table it reads
It stops all writes to the tables it has read
It forces each commit in the system to wait for it
why: VACUUM can't remove versions that an open snapshot might need. Post 14 shows it happening.

q: What's the difference between REPEATABLE READ and snapshot isolation on Postgres?
options: None: the docs say repeatable read is implemented using snapshot isolation
Snapshot isolation is stricter, and stops write skew as well
Repeatable read locks rows, and snapshot isolation doesn't
Snapshot isolation only applies to read-only transactions
why: That's why the course doesn't list it separately. In theory repeatable read means locking rows you read, and Postgres went further.

q: A session holds FOR SHARE on a row. What happens to another session's UPDATE of it?
options: It waits until the first session finishes
It fails at once with a lock error
It goes through, and the first session's read is invalidated
It's queued and applied at the next checkpoint
why: A blocked statement waits. The lecture said it gets an error, which only happens if you ask for one.

q: In Postgres, what row lock does a plain SELECT take?
options: None: it reads a snapshot, so it never blocks and is never blocked by row locks
A shared lock, released at the end of the statement
A shared lock, held until the transaction ends
An exclusive lock on the page it reads
why: Readers-block-writers belongs to lock-based designs. You only get it in Postgres by asking for FOR SHARE.

q: Where does Postgres record a row lock taken by SELECT ... FOR UPDATE?
options: In the row itself, in xmax, rather than in a lock table
In a shared hash table of every locked row
In the WAL, so that it survives a crash
In the index entry pointing at the row
why: So locking many rows doesn't use up memory, and there's no need for lock escalation as in SQL Server.

q: When does Postgres look for a deadlock?
options: When a backend has waited deadlock_timeout, 1 second by default, it checks for a cycle
Continuously, on every lock request
Once a minute, in a background process
Only when an administrator runs a check
why: The check is relatively expensive, so it only runs if a wait lasts.

q: Session A waits first, and B closes the deadlock cycle 150 ms later. Who was aborted in the real run?
options: A, because its one-second check fired after the cycle already existed
B, because the last one in always fails
Both, because Postgres aborts everyone in a cycle
Neither: the first to commit wins, and the other waits
why: The victim is whoever's check finds the cycle. 'Last one in' only held when the gap was over a second.

q: Session B inserts a key that session A inserted and hasn't committed. What decides B's result?
options: A's outcome: if A rolls back B succeeds, and if A commits B gets a duplicate key error
The order of their transaction ids: the lower id always wins
B fails immediately, whatever A does
B succeeds immediately, and A's commit then fails
why: B can't know yet whether the key is free, so it waits for A.

q: What's the best way to prevent deadlocks in an application?
options: Take locks in the same order everywhere
Raise deadlock_timeout to several minutes
Use SERIALIZABLE for every transaction
Run all writes on a single connection
why: Cycles need opposite orders. Keep a retry for error 40P01 as well, since any transaction can be a victim.

q: What does strict two-phase locking mean in practice?
options: A transaction holds all its locks until commit, so nobody reads a value that might roll back
Every lock is taken twice: once to read and once to write
Locks are released after each statement, then taken again
Two transactions take turns holding the same lock
why: The rule is to acquire, then release, and never acquire after releasing. Real databases release at the end.

q: Ana and Ben both SELECT a free seat, then UPDATE it, with no locks. What's the result?
options: Both are told they have it, and the table shows only the second name
The second UPDATE fails with a conflict error
The first UPDATE is rolled back automatically
The second SELECT waits until the first transaction commits
why: A check followed by a write isn't atomic. The second update waited, then overwrote the first.

q: Ben's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE waits behind Ana's. What does it return after Ana books the seat?
options: No rows: it re-checks the condition and the seat no longer matches
The seat as it was when Ben's query began
A deadlock error, because they wanted the same row
The seat with Ana's name, and a warning
why: The application sees zero rows and tells Ben the seat's gone.

q: Why does UPDATE ... WHERE id = 1 AND isbooked = 0 stop double booking at read committed?
options: The waiting UPDATE re-evaluates its WHERE clause on the row the first one committed
UPDATE statements run one at a time in Postgres
The WHERE clause takes a table lock for the length of the statement
Postgres compares both statements and cancels the later one
why: So the loser gets UPDATE 0. The docs describe the re-check. It's specific to this level.

q: The same UPDATE with the check runs at REPEATABLE READ. What does the second session get?
options: A serialization error, because it can't re-check against a newer row
UPDATE 0, exactly as at read committed
UPDATE 1, overwriting the first session's booking
A deadlock error after one second
why: The seat's safe either way, but the code must catch a different thing. That's the 'at the mercy of the implementation' point.

q: Which option lets a worker take the next job without waiting for rows others hold?
options: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT
SET lock_timeout = '200ms'
SELECT ... FOR SHARE
why: NOWAIT fails at once, and lock_timeout fails after a while. SKIP LOCKED returns the next free row, which is how to build a queue on a table.

q: The booking code returns early without release() when a seat is taken. With a pool of 2, what happens on the third request?
options: It times out, or hangs forever by default, because both connections are stuck idle in transaction
It works, because the pool opens a third connection when needed
It reuses one of the stuck connections, and inherits its transaction
The first two requests are cancelled to free their connections
why: The real run printed 'timeout exceeded when trying to connect'. Put release() in a finally block.

q: Why is idle in transaction worse than idle in pg_stat_activity?
options: The connection holds a transaction open, keeping its locks and stopping VACUUM cleaning up
It means the server is waiting on a disk that has stopped responding
It uses far more CPU than an active query
It means the client has crashed and the server hasn't noticed
why: It's the classic sign of a leak or a forgotten COMMIT.

q: Why does OFFSET 1000000 LIMIT 10 take so long, even with an index on the sort column?
options: It must produce every skipped row and discard it: the plan shows rows=1000010
Offsets above a million disable the index
It sorts the whole table in memory before skipping
OFFSET takes a table lock while it counts
why: An index can't jump to a position. 9,106 pages against 5 for keyset pagination.

q: A row is inserted between loading pages 1 and 2 with OFFSET. What does the reader see?
options: The last row of page 1 again at the top of page 2
An error, because the result set changed
Nothing changes: offsets are stable within a session
A gap: one row is skipped and never shown
why: Offsets count positions, so everything shifts along. Keyset pagination continues from the last row seen.

q: What do you give up with keyset pagination?
options: Jumping straight to an arbitrary page number
Sorted results
The use of an index
Consistency between pages
why: You can only move from a known row. Feeds rarely need page 500. Add the primary key as a tie-breaker on non-unique columns.

q: Why must a transaction use pool.connect() rather than pool.query() for each statement?
options: pool.query() can pick a different connection each time, and a transaction lives on one
pool.query() can't run statements that change data
pool.query() always runs in autocommit, which can't be turned off
pool.connect() opens a new TCP connection, which transactions need
why: BEGIN on one connection and UPDATE on another aren't the same transaction. Take one client, then release it.

q: What does connectionTimeoutMillis: 0 mean in node-postgres's Pool?
options: Wait forever for a free connection
Fail at once if no connection is free
Close each connection right after use
Never reuse a connection
why: The default turns a connection leak into a hang rather than an error.

q: What does a pool remove from each request's cost?
options: The TCP handshake, TLS, authentication, and starting a server process
The query's execution time on the server
The time waiting for row locks
The cost of writing to the WAL
why: Measured here: 12.63 ms per lookup with a new connection, against 1.11 ms from a pool.

q: Why isn't a bigger pool always better?
options: Real queries compete for CPU and disk, and each Postgres connection is a process
The driver slows down as the pool grows
Postgres refuses more than 100 connections from one client
Larger pools lose transactions under load
why: The chart's queries only slept, the best case for a large pool. Past some point more connections just add contention.

q: What happens to a transaction id in Postgres during a read-only transaction?
options: None is assigned until the first write
One is assigned at BEGIN, like any other
One is assigned for each statement
It borrows the id of the last committed transaction
why: pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned() stayed empty until the INSERT, so reads skip that cost anyway.

q: What's the main benefit of BEGIN READ ONLY?
options: Protection: a write inside it fails with an error
A large speed-up on every query
It stops other sessions from writing to those tables
It takes a consistent snapshot that read committed can't give
why: The real run printed 'cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction'. The optimisation is small, because Postgres already skips the id.

q: UPDATE t SET v = v + 1 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7 returns 0 rows. What does a version column tell you?
options: Someone else changed the row first: this is optimistic control done by the application
The row was deleted, and can't be updated again
The transaction was rolled back by a deadlock
A trigger rejected the update
why: No lock was held. You read the version, then detect a conflict at write time, and retry.
